J.R.R. Tolkien lived from 1892 to 1973 and was an English philologist, medievalist, and author who created Middle-earth and authored The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit. These works essentially defined modern fantasy literature. A Catholic convert and Oxford academic, he developed an entire secondary world with its own languages, histories, and mythologies, grounding his fiction in scholarly rigor and deep knowledge of Northern European mythology and medieval literature. His work elevated fantasy from children's literature to a serious literary art form.

Tolkien was a philologist and medievalist scholar. His fiction grew from linguistic and mythological interests rather than pure imagination. The Hobbit, published in 1937, began as a story for his children and features Bilbo Baggins and his quest to reclaim a dragon's gold. It established many conventions of heroic fantasy. The Lord of the Rings, published from 1954 to 1955, is his masterwork, a trilogy epic of unprecedented scope. It follows Frodo Baggins through Middle-earth as he seeks to destroy a ring of power.

Tolkien created an entirely constructed mythology. The Silmarillion contains the history of the First Age, the creation myth and fall of the Elves, and the theological framework of his world. His languages, especially Elvish, were constructed with linguistic discipline. They were not mere ornamentation but the expressive core of his creative vision. Tolkien consciously worked in the tradition of medieval literature and Norse mythology, embedding allusions and structures from Beowulf, The Kalevala, and Germanic sagas. His work influenced virtually all subsequent fantasy literature.

The archetype of the quest, the fellowship, the dark lord, and the magic ring all became standard because of Tolkien. The Lord of the Rings stands as his masterwork and the foundational epic of modern fantasy. The Hobbit is the earlier, more accessible adventure that introduced many elements developed in The Lord of the Rings. Fantasy as a literary genre was elevated through Tolkien's scholarly depth and imaginative scope. The Hobbit began as children's literature but transcended the category. Odin, the Norse god whose figure as a wandering, disguised sage influences Gandalf, is central to understanding Tolkien's sources. Middle-earth is the secondary world Tolkien created. His life's work was building its history, languages, and lore. Beowulf, the medieval poem Tolkien studied and whose traditions he consciously extended, shapes the underlying architecture of his mythology.
